cognate: *h₁ógʷʰi- 'snake' (Ved. áhi- = Gk ὄφις) + *ǵerh₂- 'grow old' (Ved. jūrṇá- 'aged, worn out' ~ Gk γῆρας 'old age') used of the snake's cast skin; *serp- 'creep' in the context (Ved. sarpati; Gk ἕρπουσιν in the paired Aristotle passage)
drift_or_renewal: Greek lexicalises the *ǵerh₂- noun itself as the name of the slough (τὸ καλούμενον γῆρας, 'the so-called old age'), where Vedic keeps adjective + noun (jūrṇā́ tvác- 'aged skin'). The verb of shedding is renewed: Ved. áti sarp- 'creep out beyond' / later hā-, nir-muc-; Gk ἐκδύνω / ἀποδύομαι. Latin senecta / senectus 'cast skin of a snake' (Pliny) would be a third, renewed (*sen-) reflex. That is recalled, not checked locally, and not used as evidence here
shared_syntax: a simile with the snake as comparandum: Ved. áhiḥ ná ... (nom. + ná) vs Gk ὥσπερ οἱ ὄφεις ...; the cast skin is the object of a verb of leaving or shedding: jūrṇā́m ... tvácam (acc.) vs τὸ ... γῆρας (acc.)
context: RV 9.86.44: Soma runs through the filter and leaves his husk behind 'as a snake creeps out of its aged skin'. HA 5.17: crustaceans shed their shell in spring 'as snakes do the so-called old age'. Both are illustrative similes on moulting. Each tradition also links moulting with the casting off of old age or evil: AB 6.1 says the snakes, 'having left the former aged skin, go forth with a new one', and are freed of evil; Lucian has snakes 'stripping off old age'; Homer and H.Ven. have 'scraping old age off' (γῆρας ἀποξύσας) for rejuvenation. That treats old age as a removable outer layer
phrase: *h₁ógʷʰis ... *ǵerh₂- (skin) — 'the snake (casts off) its old age / aged skin'

cognate: genitive *diw-ós / *diw-és of the sky god (Ved. diváḥ = Gk Διός) qualifying the word for rain
drift_or_renewal: The head noun is renewed. Vedic uses vr̥ṣṭí- 'rain' (also rétas- 'seed, outflow', as in the pivot). Greek uses ὄμβρος, whose Vedic cognate abhrá- means 'rain-cloud'; RV 5.63.4c has abhréṇa vr̥ṣṭyā́ next to diví. In Vedic div- is both 'sky' and the god Dyaus, while Greek has the personal god
shared_syntax: adnominal genitive of *dyew- + rain noun; often as the agent of growth or swelling. Od. 9.111 'Διὸς ὄμβρος ἀέξει' (the rain of Zeus makes [the vines] grow) ~ RV 2.27.15b 'diváḥ vr̥ṣṭím ... púṣyan' (making the rain of heaven thrive) and 5.63.1d 'vr̥ṣṭíḥ ... pinvate diváḥ' (the rain of heaven swells)
context: Il. 11.493: a winter torrent rushes down the mountains 'driven by the rain of Zeus' (simile). RV 9.74.1c: Soma, the steed, unites with 'the outflow of heaven' that swells the milk. In 16 RV padas Soma or the gods are asked to make 'the rain of heaven' flow (pári srava, pavasva). In both traditions the formula describes rain as coming from the sky god, applied to streams and abundance. The genitive is formally identical (diváḥ = Διός). The Greek formula recurs 5 times and the Vedic one is a stock phrase
phrase: *diwós + rain noun: 'the rain of Sky/Zeus' (diváḥ vr̥ṣṭí- ~ Διὸς ὄμβρος)

cognate: polar pair *ǵʰeym- 'cold/winter' + *gʷʰer- 'heat' (Ved. hím-/himá- ~ Gk χεῖμα/χειμών; Ved. ghr̥ṇá-/gharmá- ~ Gk θέρος, θερμός)
drift_or_renewal: Greek has narrowed both terms to seasons ('winter' / 'summer'), while Vedic keeps the qualities ('cold' / 'heat'). The *gʷʰer- term has different formations: Ved. ghr̥ṇá- or gharmá- (= Gk θερμός), Gk θέρος (= Ved. háras-, which is not used in the pair)
shared_syntax: two coordinated or anaphoric members in the same case: Ved. śám himā́ śám ghr̥ṇéna (instr.), hiména gharmám; Gk τοῦ χειμῶνος ... τοῦ θέρους (gen. of time), χείματος οὐδὲ θέρευς, χεῖμα καὶ θέρος
context: RV 10.37.10: a blessing that runs through all conditions (light, day, cold, heat, road, home). Greek uses the pair as a merism for 'at all times, in all conditions': Xen. Cyr. 'neither shiver in winter nor swelter in summer', Od. 7.118 'neither in winter nor in summer', Hes. Op. 640. The pairing of cold and heat is natural and could have arisen independently. The claim is only that the same two roots carry the polar figure in both branches

support.locus: Vedic prose (DCS): 'āpnoty amṛtatvam akṣitaṃ svarge loke'; 'karma akṣitam amṛtam vyoma'

drift_or_renewal: In the anchor Od. 11.330 the pair appears inverted rather than as a coordination: νὺξ ... ἄμβροτος with the positive verb φθῖτο ('the immortal night would waste away'). The privative coordination is found elsewhere in Greek with ἀθάνατος, which renews ἄμβροτος: ἀθάνατον ἄφθιτόν τε (Eur.), ἀθάνατοι ... ἄφθιτοι (H.Merc.)
shared_syntax: two privative adjectives of the same referent: Ved. amŕ̥te loké ákṣite (loc. agreement, noun framed by the adjectives) ~ Gk ἀθάνατον ἄφθιτόν τε (acc. coordination); in Od. 11.330 an adjective of the night plus the verb of the second root
context: RV 9.113.7: the poet asks to be placed in the immortal, imperishable world of light, the heaven of the blessed dead. The Greek privative pair describes the gods or deification (Eur. Andr.: Peleus made 'immortal and imperishable'). Od. 11.330 comes in the Nekyia, but its pairing is ad hoc. This is weak: coordinating near-synonymous privatives is a common figure, and the better-known inherited pair is *n̥-mr̥tó- + *n̥-ǵerh₂- (ajára- ~ ἀγήρως)

support.locus: Slovo o polku Igoreve, opening (TOROT spi, sentence 2)

cognate: *tekʷ- 'run, rush' (Ved. √tak-, taktá- ~ ORus. течи, потещи, дотечи, растекатися) as the verb of similes of rapid motion with a bird of prey and a wild beast
drift_or_renewal: The animals are renewed. Ved. śyená- 'falcon' ~ ORus. соколъ / орелъ (not cognate). Ved. mr̥gá- 'wild beast' ~ ORus. вълкъ 'wolf' (a cognate of Ved. vŕ̥ka-, which is not used here). In Slavic *tekʷ- is the ordinary 'run/flow' verb, whereas Vedic √tak- is rare (5 RV padas) and confined to swift horses, beasts and falcons
shared_syntax: simile of manner on a motion verb: Ved. N-nom. ná taktáḥ arṣati ('rushes, swift like a falcon / beast') ~ ORus. instrumental of comparison + *tekʷ- verb (влъкомъ потече 'ran as a wolf'). In the Slovo the paired animal similes (wolf on the earth, eagle or falcon in the sky) attach to *tekʷ- compounds
context: RV: Soma rushes to the vessel like a falcon or like a wild beast. Slovo: Igor escapes 'as a falcon' while Ovlur 'ran as a wolf'; Boyan 'spread (растекашется) as a grey wolf over the earth, as a dusky eagle under the clouds'; Boyan's falcons 'overtake' (дотечаше) the swans. Both are poetic registers with paired predator similes of speed. This is weak. *tekʷ- is a basic verb in Slavic and predator similes for speed are universal, so chance is likely
phrase: *tekʷ- + simile 'rush like a falcon / like a wild beast (wolf)'
